article.title: The Impact of ICE
article.author: Guest Author
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A mother detained while seeking her green card. A woman arrested outside her home in pajamas and slippers. A transgender immigrant forced to choose between prolonged isolation and the threat of violence. A 60-year-old woman imprisoned for months after immigration agents allegedly mistook her for a 25-year-old. These were not hypothetical scenarios. They were among the experiences described by immigrant rights advocates at the fourth annual Left Coast Forum , held October 2–4, 2026, at California State University, Los Angeles. The panel, “The Impact of ICE: The Fight to Shut Down the Concentration Camps in California,” brought together organizers confronting the expansion of immigration detention, the growing influence of private prison corporations, and the erosion of constitutional protections. Facilitated by NO Concentration Camps CA and moderated by artist and activist MaryLinda Moss , the discussion featured Jeannie Parent , coordinator of Kern Welcoming and Extending Solidarity to Immigrants (KWESI); Bertie Hernandez , an undocumented transgender organizer working with the Dignity Not Detention Coalition; and Cal Soto , Workers’ Rights Director and Staff Attorney at the National Day Laborer Organizing Network (NDLON). Together, they described a system they believe is designed not simply to detain immigrants, but to extract profit from their incarceration while making resistance increasingly difficult. Families Torn Apart, Lives Put on Hold Jeannie Parent has been visiting people in immigration detention since 2015, when the Mesa Verde detention facility opened in Bakersfield. Through KWESI, volunteers visit incarcerated immigrants, provide money for food and telephone calls, and help arrange transportation, clothing, and shelter when people are released. Parent described a woman from Utah who was detained after stepping outside her home in pajamas and slippers. She had been caring for a daughter undergoing cancer treatment and a husband recovering from a kidney transplant. She spent eight months detained in California City. Another woman came from India on a student visa, earned a nursing degree, married, and had a baby. During an interview concerning her immigration status, she was separated from her husband, handcuffed, and detained for eight months. When released, she told Parent that she was grateful she had introduced her six-month-old baby to bottle-feeding before her arrest, allowing her family to care for the child. Parent rejected the government's portrayal of detained immigrants as the "worst of the worst." "These are nursing mothers, our neighbors, our friends," she told the audience. During the first seven months of 2026, Parent reported, KWESI provided $50 commissary deposits to approximately 700 people and helped more than 200 individuals through visits and other assistance. When Human Confinement Becomes a Business The panelists repeatedly returned to the financial incentives sustaining immigration detention. Companies such as GEO Group and CoreCivic operate detention facilities under government contracts, creating a system in which public money supports privately operated incarceration. According to the panelists, people held inside face inadequate food, expensive communications, restrictive visitation, and considerable obstacles to obtaining legal assistance. Parent described California City's detention facility, which she said held at least 2,200 people, as operating much like a maximum-security prison. The financial exploitation continues even after release. Soto described people leaving detention without telephones, transportation, or money, sometimes after spending months purchasing necessities from prison commissaries. The contradiction is especially troubling for advocates. They raise money to help people survive confinement, knowing some of those funds ultimately benefit the companies operating the facilities. The panelists argued that this arrangement creates a disturbing incentive: The longer people remain incarcerated, the more money detention operators may receive. A Transgender Organizer Confronts the System That Imprisoned Them For Bertie Hernandez, immigration detention is not an abstract political issue. Hernandez described spending approximately four months detained at Adelanto during Donald Trump's first administration. As a transgender person, Hernandez confronted an impossible choice: Accept isolation for approximately 23 hours each day or enter a detention population where their personal safety could be threatened. Hernandez chose the latter, explaining that prolonged isolation posed its own profound psychological dangers. That experience helped shape their commitment to organizing alongside detained transgender, queer, and gender-variant immigrants. Hernandez challenged the assumption that the system could be repaired simply through better management or improved detention conditions. From their feminist abolitionist perspective, the problem is structural. Racism, economic exploitation, gender-based violence, and incarceration reinforce one another. Rather than asking the public to recognize the humanity of immigrants, Hernandez turned the question around: Why must incarcerated people continually prove they deserve humane treatment? The moral responsibility, they suggested, rests with those willing to tolerate their mistreatment. Fighting ICE in Court—and Beyond Cal Soto described how NDLON, a national network of more than 70 day laborer worker centers, has expanded its work from fighting wage theft and workplace exploitation to challenging immigration raids and detention. Soto discussed litigation involving warrantless arrests and discriminatory immigration enforcement practices. In one case, a federal judge ordered the release of a 60-year-old woman who had been detained since April. According to Soto, government records indicated that agents were looking for someone approximately 25 years old. Soto also discussed litigation challenging immigration enforcement practices in Southern California, including raids targeting day laborers. The legal campaign incorporated more than 100 declarations from people describing their encounters with immigration agents. Importantly, Soto emphasized that the affected workers were participants in developing the litigation strategy, not merely witnesses called upon to support attorneys' arguments. Although courts have sometimes provided meaningful relief, Soto warned against depending on judges alone to protect vulnerable communities. Legal victories matter, but organized communities make those victories possible—and help turn individual cases into broader campaigns for justice. What Can One Person Do? Perhaps the most practical discussion came when an audience member asked how organizers should respond to people who feel overwhelmed, emotionally exhausted, or powerless. Parent suggested beginning with something as simple as writing a letter to a detained immigrant. For someone who has spent months without receiving a visitor, a letter can provide reassurance that the outside world has not forgotten them. Other opportunities include contributing commissary funds, providing transportation after release, creating artwork for demonstrations, contacting elected officials, or participating in organized protests. Hernandez emphasized that anger need not lead to helplessness. It can become a force for action and transformation. Soto offered another perspective: Effective movements require discipline and continuity, not simply moments of inspiration. He compared organizing to a musical composition containing notes too long for one singer to sustain. Another voice must enter as the first falls silent. The movement continues because people support one another. From Individual Resistance to Collective Power As the discussion concluded, Moss emphasized the importance of connecting organizations across California, building coalitions, and sustaining public pressure against detention facilities. The organizers made clear that the fight is not simply about improving conditions inside immigration detention centers. Their objective is to shut them down. But their work also poses a broader question: What does it say about a society when incarcerating people generates corporate profits while providing adequate food, housing, healthcare, and legal representation remains a struggle? The panel offered no easy solution to a system sustained by enormous political and economic power. Instead, it presented something more practical: a model of resistance built through collective action, mutual aid, legal challenges, public education, and solidarity with those most directly harmed. The session ended with a call-and-response that captured its central message: “What's stronger than a fascist?” “The power of the masses!”
